title: Crashtroid - Preventing Ear Fatigue with Roguelike Music
speaker: Crashtroid (Adam)
summary: Crashtroid, composer for Peglin, offers anecdotal strategies to keep roguelike players, who hear the same tracks across many runs, from developing ear fatigue. His three main points are unique segmentation within a loop so it feels like it progresses (illustrated with The Binding of Isaac's 'Repentant' and Peglin's final-stage theme), pacing music to the gameplay rather than only the aesthetic (contrasting Roboquest and Risk of Rain 2), and smooth transitions and flow using ambient/combat variants, shared motifs and stingers (with a flowchart of Hades' stage music). He closes with a test: if you can't listen to a track for 15 minutes outside the game, it won't work inside it.

insights.claim: Because roguelikes are replayed many times, their music is especially prone to causing ear fatigue, where repeated listening blurs sounds together and tires the player.
insights.detail: Crashtroid defines ear fatigue as hearing something so often or so loud that frequencies blur and become hard to distinguish, as composers experience when looping a section while mixing. He wants players to stay engaged with the art across runs, like not being worn out by a shop theme heard a million times.
insights.quote: A roguelike is a game someone will play over and over, ear fatigue is libel to occur to them and you don't really want that to happen

insights.claim: Roguelike music loops should contain distinctly segmented sections so the player feels progress through the loop rather than having it meld into the background.
insights.detail: Sections can be classic intro/chorus structure or even swapping songs midway with a radio system. In The Binding of Isaac's 'Repentant', four sections add chords, then vocals, then a piano ending that lifts to a major chord suggesting a chance to survive.
insights.quote: the player upon hearing this loop is feeling like there is progress being made rather than having it meld into the background

insights.claim: Peglin's final-stage theme uses subtle segmentation by changing the solo instrument and drum line between sections.
insights.detail: Crashtroid notes key changes or any other variation can also distinguish sections; Peglin's are more subtle than Isaac's.
insights.quote: the different changes I have made were changing the solo instrument, changes in the drum line

insights.claim: Roguelike music should be paced to the moment-to-moment gameplay, not only the game's aesthetic, ideally informed by the composer playing a prototype.
insights.detail: The main thing players do is play, and their actions shape how they perceive audio. Knowing how the game feels helps write music that fits it.
insights.quote: the main thing the player is doing with your game is playing it. The actions they take every moment of their journey through your game

insights.claim: Roboquest's fast arena-shooter music lines up with bunny hopping and gun fire rates (the speaker doesn't know if by coincidence), while Risk of Rain 2's music emphasises exploration and discovery on a sprawling alien planet.
insights.detail: Both are combat shooter roguelikes, yet their composers made very different music to match how each plays: Roboquest's prespawned arenas versus Risk of Rain 2's searching for enemies and loot.
insights.quote: the guns fire rates really line up with the beats per minute of a lot of the songs in the game

insights.claim: Avoiding jarring music cuts across long or repeated runs helps maintain flow, using fading alternate versions of tracks (ambient/combat) and shared motifs across an area.
insights.detail: Crashtroid cites speedrunners and three-hour runs. Borderlands is an example of combat and ambient variants; map areas can share a melody in a cut-down passive version for cohesion.
insights.quote: Not having that jarring transition between songs is really helpful to maintain that sense of flow

insights.claim: Hades' stage music fades between ambient and combat versions, then uses stingers and silence before new tracks to quietly signal progress through a floor.
insights.detail: As Crashtroid perceives it, a stinger concludes the song, silence follows until the next room where a new song signals the 33% mark; the pattern repeats after the miniboss and boss. He recommends flowcharting music like this to find gaps that break immersion.
insights.quote: It is a quiet way of telling the player they are making progress

insights.claim: A practical test for roguelike music: if you can't listen to a track for 15 minutes outside the game, it probably won't work in the game.
insights.detail: Crashtroid's closing advice after restating segmentation, pacing and flow.
insights.quote: If you can't listen to the song more than 15 minutes at a time outside the game it probably won't work inside the game
